To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The more complex the causal explanations that subjects construct to explain a particular outcome, the more likely they will judge the outcome to be probable.

the likelihood of a known outcome and the causal attributions that follow are affected by the number of causal explanations subjects construct and by the number of outcome possibilities subjects consider.

(a) the more causal antecedents that are provided to subjects, the more likely they are to explain an outcome and the more likely they will attribute the outcome to the antecedents, and (b) the more outcome alternatives that subjects are induced to consider, the less likely they are to attribute the outcome to a particular antecedent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people explain and evaluate the outcomes of social interactions and with the consequences of these explanations for social judgment and decision making.
how the human mind constructs explanations when attempting to link events.
how people explain and predict outcomes, particularly when they are aware that the outcome did or did not occur.

the present research demonstrates that the causal explanations subjects construct when linking antecendents to outcomes at enconding can account for both hindsight effects and biased attributions.

the results are consistent with the notion that hindsight bias and the fundamental attribution error are manifestations of the same basic cognitive processes, namely, the construction of causal explanations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
people tend to exaggerate the probability of an outcome and its causal origins.
hindsight and causal attribution biases are the product of a single cognitive mechanism: causal explanation.
hindsight bias is a function of the complexity of subjects causal explanation of the outcome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the more we know, the less likely it is we are going to make errors.
the hindsight bias can be reduced by encouraging people to consider alternative outcomes.
the more complex and varied our causal explanations, the less we tend to exaggerate the probability of the known outcomes.
